Monotheism is the belief that there is exactly one God — and only one. Not two, not many, not none. One single divine being who created everything and governs all of existence. That is the foundation of the whole idea. If you hold this belief, you are a monotheist, and the system of thought or religion built around it is called monotheism.
The nature of this one God

In monotheism, this single God is not merely the most powerful being among many. This God is understood to be in a category entirely of their own — unlimited and unlike anything else that exists. Typically, this God is described as all-powerful (able to do anything), all-knowing (aware of everything — past, present, and future), and present everywhere simultaneously (not confined to one location). This God is also considered the creator of the entire universe — the one who brought everything into existence from nothing.

Crucially, the God of monotheism is almost always understood as a personal God — meaning a being with will, intention, and the capacity to have a relationship with people. This is an important detail. The God of monotheism is a who, not a what — not a vague cosmic energy or an abstract force, but a being who acts, communicates, cares, and is involved in the lives of people. This God is also typically regarded as the source of morality — the ultimate standard of right and wrong comes from this one God.

The three most recognized monotheistic religions in the world are Judaism, Christianity, and Islam — sometimes collectively called the Abrahamic faiths because all three trace their roots to the figure of Abraham.

Judaism is considered one of the earliest recorded monotheistic religions in human history. It holds that there is one God — often referred to as Yahweh or Jehovah — who entered into a special relationship with the Jewish people and revealed moral and spiritual law to them, most famously through the Ten Commandments.

Christianity shares Judaism's commitment to one God but introduces a concept called the Trinity — the belief that the one God exists as three distinct persons: the Father, the Son (Jesus Christ), and the Holy Spirit. Christians maintain that this is still monotheism — not three gods, but one God expressed in three persons. This is admittedly a more complex and philosophical form of the belief, and it has been debated and refined over centuries of theological thought.

Islam may be the strictest expression of monotheism among the major world religions. It places absolute, uncompromising emphasis on the oneness and uniqueness of God — referred to as Allah, which simply means "God" in Arabic. Islam has a central doctrine called Tawhid, which means the absolute unity and singularity of God, with no partners, no equals, no intermediaries sharing in divinity whatsoever.

Other monotheistic religions include Sikhism, which holds a strong belief in one formless God, and the Bahá'í Faith, which also centers on one God while emphasizing the unity of all religions.
Understanding monotheism by contrast — what it is not

The clearest way to sharpen your understanding of monotheism is to see how it differs from other belief systems.

Polytheism is the belief in many gods. The ancient Greeks worshipped Zeus, Athena, Apollo, Poseidon, and dozens of others — each ruling over a specific domain like the sea, wisdom, or the sun. The ancient Romans, Norse, Egyptians, and many other civilizations held similar beliefs. In polytheism, no single god is absolute — the gods often compete, quarrel, and have limited power relative to each other.

Atheism is the absence of belief in any god at all. An atheist does not think any divine being exists.

Agnosticism is a position of uncertainty. An agnostic does not make a firm claim either way — neither confidently believing in God nor confidently denying God's existence, holding that the question may be unknowable.

Deism is the belief that one God created the universe but then stepped entirely back, leaving it to run on its own without any continued involvement. A deist's God is sometimes compared to a watchmaker who built the watch and wound it up — then walked away. So while deism is technically a form of one-God belief, it differs from mainstream monotheism in denying any ongoing relationship between God and humanity.

Pantheism is the belief that God and the universe are not separate — they are one and the same thing. God is not a being who made the universe; God is the universe itself. This is very different from monotheism, where God is a distinct being who exists separately from and above creation.

Henotheism is a subtler distinction worth knowing. A henotheist worships one god as their primary or personal god but does not deny that other gods may exist. It is like saying, "I follow my god, but your god may be real too." This is different from monotheism, which makes an absolute claim — there is only one God in total existence, and no others exist at all.

Even within monotheism, not everyone understands the "oneness" of God in exactly the same way. Islam draws the hardest line — God is one, indivisible, with no shared divine nature whatsoever. Judaism is similarly strict about God's singularity, rejecting any idea of God having distinct "persons." Christianity, with its Trinity, holds a more layered understanding — one God, but three persons — which some critics (including Muslims and Jews) argue complicates the claim to pure monotheism, while Christians themselves firmly insist their belief is still monotheism properly understood.

This shows that monotheism is not a single rigid box — it is a broad category defined by the core commitment to one God, but with meaningful variation in how that commitment is expressed and understood.

Monotheism has shaped human civilization more than almost any other idea in history. Today, the majority of the world's population belongs to a monotheistic religion, meaning billions of people build their entire sense of morality, purpose, and meaning around the belief in one God.

Because this one God is understood as the God of everyone — not the patron deity of one tribe or city — monotheism carries a universalist claim: the same God applies to all people everywhere, which has made it a powerfully unifying (and at times, divisive) force throughout history. It has influenced laws, ethics, philosophy, art, politics, and science across thousands of years in ways that are difficult to overstate.

On a personal level, monotheism creates a uniquely intimate dimension to religious life. If there is only one God, and that God created you specifically and knows you fully, then your relationship with the divine is direct, personal, and unmediated by a crowd of competing deities. This sense of a one-on-one relationship between a person and the one God is one of monotheism's most defining emotional and spiritual characteristics.
